The distance measure defines what it means for the values of two raster cells to be similar.
Therefore, the choice of a distance measure is crucial for the supercell segmentation results, and the decision of which measure to use should be based on the characteristics of the input data and the goals of the analysis. 
This vignette provides an overview of the available distance measures, their requirements, and guidance for selecting an appropriate measure for your analysis.
It also includes a short example comparing three different measures on a sample raster dataset.

```{r}
#| message: false
library(supercells)
library(terra)
```

# Available measures

To check the available distance measures, use the `sc_list_distances()` function.
It returns a data frame with the information on the measure names, accepted input types, what the measure compares, the effect of layer rescaling, and guidance for choosing the measure.
Below is a summary of the available measures, grouped by the type of input they accept.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
distances <- sc_list_distances()

for (input in unique(distances$input)) {
  current <- distances[distances$input == input, ]
  shown <- current[c(
    "name", "compares", "effect_of_layer_rescaling", "guidance"
  )]
  names(shown) <- c(
    "Name", "What it compares", "Layer rescaling", "Guidance"
  )

  cat("## Input: ", tools::toTitleCase(input), "\n\n", sep = "")
  print(knitr::kable(shown, row.names = FALSE))
  cat("\n\n")
}
```

# Choosing a measure

| Data or similarity question | Measures to consider |
|---|---|
| Absolute differences across comparable numeric layers matter | `euclidean` if larger differences should count more, or `manhattan` for linear contributions |
| The largest difference in any one layer should dominate | `chebyshev` |
| Relative differences within individual layers matter | `canberra`; for nonnegative data, `wavehedges` or `clark` |
| Overall difference relative to the complete profile matters | `soergel` or `czekanowski` |
| Relative pattern matters, not the overall magnitude of the profile | `cosine_distance` |
| Each cell contains class probabilities summing to 1 | `jsd` or `non-intersection` |
| Layers are an ordered one-dimensional sequence | `dtw` |
| Layers contain the coordinates of a two-dimensional trajectory | `dtw2d` |

These are starting points rather than automatic choices. When layer rescaling
can change a measure, put layers on comparable scales unless different influence
is intentional. Retune `compactness` after changing the distance measure.

For probability measures, normalize every cell to sum to 1 and use mean
centres. For `dtw`, arrange layers in sequence order. For `dtw2d`, arrange
layers by dimension, with sequence order within each dimension.

-->

# Comparing three measures

We illustrate segmentations obtained with three distance measures: `euclidean`, `canberra`, and `cosine_distance`. 
Each measure is tuned separately because their distance values have different scales.

```{r}
ortho <- rast(system.file("raster/ortho.tif", package = "supercells"))
ortho <- aggregate(ortho, fact = 2)

tune_euclidean <- sc_tune_compactness(ortho, step = 10, dist_fun = "euclidean")
sc_euclidean <- sc_slic(
  ortho,
  step = 10,
  compactness = tune_euclidean$compactness,
  dist_fun = "euclidean"
)

tune_canberra <- sc_tune_compactness(ortho, step = 10, dist_fun = "canberra")
sc_canberra <- sc_slic(
  ortho,
  step = 10,
  compactness = tune_canberra$compactness,
  dist_fun = "canberra"
)

tune_cosine <- sc_tune_compactness(ortho, step = 10, dist_fun = "cosine_distance")
sc_cosine <- sc_slic(
  ortho,
  step = 10,
  compactness = tune_cosine$compactness,
  dist_fun = "cosine_distance"
)
```

```{r, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4}
#| echo: false
results <- list(
  euclidean = sc_euclidean,
  canberra = sc_canberra,
  cosine_distance = sc_cosine
)

for (measure in names(results)) {
  plotRGB(ortho, scale = 255, axes = FALSE, main = measure)
  plot(results[[measure]][0], add = TRUE, border = "white", lwd = 0.75)
}
```

Each measure produces a different segmentation of the raster dataset:

- Euclidean distance responds to absolute RGB differences. 
- Canberra distance compares channel differences relative to their values. 
- Cosine distance compares the RGB profile while ignoring its overall magnitude.

# Custom measures

Other measures can be supplied as functions.
A custom function must take two numeric vectors and return one finite, nonnegative value, with smaller values meaning greater similarity.

For example, Minkowski distance with $p = 3$ gives large layer differences more influence than Euclidean distance ($p = 2$); Chebyshev distance is the limiting case as $p$ approaches infinity.

```{r}
minkowski3 <- function(x, y) {
  sum(abs(x - y)^3)^(1 / 3)
}

tune_minkowski3 <- sc_tune_compactness(
  ortho,
  step = 10,
  dist_fun = minkowski3
)

sc_minkowski3 <- sc_slic(
  ortho,
  step = 10,
  compactness = tune_minkowski3$compactness,
  dist_fun = minkowski3
)
```

```{r, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4}
#| echo: false
plotRGB(ortho, scale = 255, axes = FALSE, main = "Minkowski distance (p = 3)")
plot(sc_minkowski3[0], add = TRUE, border = "white", lwd = 0.75)
```
